title: Ground station audio
description:
One object per audio frame - stream `a` on the relay (transport.md).

Opus, because this is the platform's largest single consumer and the link is metered. Uncompressed 24 kHz 16-bit mono is 384 kbit/s, and base64 inside a JSON envelope made it ~512; Opus at 16-24 kbit/s is transparent for voice and reaches the same console for roughly a twelfth of the bandwidth at the batch size suggested below - a twentieth only at 16 kbit/s and the maximum batch, which costs two seconds of latency on a push-to-talk channel. That saving is the whole reason this stream is shaped the way it is, and it is why the format is fixed here rather than left to a station.

Published ONLY when both gates are open: the squelch is open, AND the platform has asked within a live `radio.audio` lease. A station nobody has asked sends nothing at all. See contract/transport.md.

codec.description: Always `opus` in this version. A string rather than a closed enum precisely so a future codec is the additive change this field exists to allow - a validator that rejected an unknown value would make that promise false, and every consumer validates. **A consumer that does not recognise the value must drop the frame**, not attempt to decode it: unlike a telemetry field, guessing here produces noise in somebody's ear.

rate.description: Sample rate in Hz that the packets decode to. Opus works internally at 48 kHz and resamples, so this is what the decoder should be configured for, not a property of the encoder. 24000 suits airband voice; the console resamples to whatever the browser grants. Enumerated rather than ranged because Opus supports exactly these five.

channels.description: Mono. Airband is one channel of one receiver, and stereo would double the cost of the stream this schema exists to make cheap.

frame_ms.description: Duration each packet decodes to. Uniform across a message, so a consumer can size its buffer from packet count without inspecting them. 20 is the usual choice for voice: shorter costs proportionally more header, longer costs latency and loses more audio per dropped packet.

packets.description:
Whole Opus packets, in order, each base64 of one packet. Raw packets, NOT Ogg- or WebM-encapsulated: a browser decodes these directly with WebCodecs, and a container here would have to be stripped by whoever consumes them.

An array rather than one concatenated blob because Opus packets are variable length and self-delimiting only inside a container - carrying them as separate strings means no length prefixes to agree on and no framing to get wrong. Base64 costs a third of the audio bytes, which is about 21% of a whole message once the envelope is counted; against a codec saving of an order of magnitude that is a trade worth making to keep the envelope JSON. Binary frames on the relay would save a further third and are a transport change rather than a schema one.

**Batch at least 4 packets, and 8 is the sensible default.** The fixed overhead is ~198 bytes per message whatever the contents, and an Opus packet at 24 kbit/s is only 60: one packet per message costs 112 kbit/s to carry a 24 kbit/s codec, which is most of the saving thrown away. Eight packets of 20 ms is 160 ms of audio for ~865 bytes on the wire, or 43 kbit/s. The arithmetic lives in transport.md; if these ever disagree, that one is right.

seq.description: Message counter, increasing by one, wrapping at 2^32. Optional, and the reason to send it: this transport is explicitly droppable, so a console that receives seq 41 after seq 39 knows a chunk was lost and can conceal the gap rather than playing the next audio as though it were continuous. Without it, loss is inaudible to the consumer and sounds like a glitch to the listener. Resets when a station restarts.
